1H (Number Theory)

Words: 242 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 242
1H OurBigBook.com
Put e=(N−1)/2. The odd integer N is an Euler pseudoprime to the coprime base b when
be≡(Nb​)(modN),
(1)
where (b/N) is the Jacobi symbol.
Let G=(Z/NZ)× be the unit group of residue classes modulo N, and partition it into the set E of bases satisfying the displayed congruence and the set W of Euler witnesses that do not. If b0​∈W, multiplication by b0​ maps E injectively into W: indeed, if b∈E and bb0​ also lay in E, then the multiplicativity of the Jacobi symbol would give
beb0e​≡(Nb​)(Nb0​​)(modN).
(2)
Cancelling the invertible congruence for b would say that b0​∈E, a contradiction. Hence ∣W∣≥∣E∣, so at least half of the coprime bases are witnesses.
It remains to construct one witness for every odd composite number N. If N is not squarefree, choose an odd prime number p with p2∣N. The Chinese remainder theorem gives a unit b such that b≡1+p(modpa) for the full power pa∣N and b≡1 modulo every other prime-power factor. The binomial theorem gives
be≡(1+p)e≡1+ep(modp2).
(3)
Since p∤e, this is neither 1 nor −1 modulo p2, whereas the Jacobi symbol is always 1 or −1. Thus b is a witness.
If N is squarefree and composite, choose distinct primes p,q∣N. By the Chinese remainder theorem, choose b to be a quadratic nonresidue modulo p and to satisfy b≡1 modulo every other prime divisor of N. Then (b/N)=−1, while be≡1(modq), so the Euler congruence again fails. This proves the existence of an Euler witness for every odd composite integer.

2H (Topics in Analysis)

Words: 199 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 199
2H OurBigBook.com
The polynomial Runge theorem says that if K⊂C is compact, C∖K is connected, and f is holomorphic on a neighbourhood of K, then for every ε>0 there is a polynomial p such that supz∈K​∣p(z)−f(z)∣<ε.
For an explicit approximation on the left semicircle K={z:∣z∣=1,Rez≤0}, define
pn​(z)=−41​∑j=0n​∑k=0n2​(kj+k​)(4z​)k.
(4)
The two power-series expansions
z1​=∑j=0∞​(z−4)j+1(−4)j​,(z−4)j+11​=(−4)j+11​∑k=0∞​(kj+k​)(4z​)k
(5)
produce this formula. The first is a geometric series whose ratio has modulus at most 4/17​<1 on K. The second converges uniformly on the whole unit circle; the elementary bound (kj+k​)≤2j+k shows that truncating it at k=n2 gives a total error tending to zero even after summing over 0≤j≤n. Consequently pn​→1/z uniformly on K. This is an explicit polynomial approximation of the reciprocal on the left semicircle.
No such sequence exists on the punctured unit circle S={z:∣z∣=1,z=1}. If polynomials pn​ converged uniformly there, they would be Uniformly Cauchy. Continuity gives
sup∣z∣=1​∣pn​(z)−pm​(z)∣=supz∈S​∣pn​(z)−pm​(z)∣,
(6)
so they would converge uniformly on the entire unit circle. The uniform limit theorem would force the value at the missing point to be 1, and hence the limit would be 1/z on the full circle. But the Cauchy integral theorem gives ∮pn​(z)dz=0 for every n, while uniform convergence and contour integration would imply
0=limn→∞​∮pn​(z)dz=∮zdz​=2πi,
(7)
a contradiction. This is the polynomial approximation obstruction on a punctured circle.

3I (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 145 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 145
3I OurBigBook.com
Use Shamir's secret sharing over the finite field Fp​. The Chair independently chooses a1​,…,ar−1​ from the uniform distribution on a finite set Fp​ and forms the random polynomial
f(X)=N+a1​X+⋯+ar−1​Xr−1∈Fp​[X].
(8)
Choose distinct nonzero x1​,…,xs​∈Fp​, with s equal to the number of discs to be issued, and inscribe (xi​,f(xi​)) on disc i.
Any r discs give r distinct values of a polynomial of degree at most r−1. Their Vandermonde determinant is nonzero, so polynomial interpolation recovers f uniquely and hence recovers the secret as N=f(0).
Conversely, fix any r−1 observed discs and any candidate secret n∈Fp​. Interpolating through those r−1 points and (0,n) gives exactly one polynomial of degree at most r−1. Thus every candidate n is compatible with the observed discs in exactly the same number of ways. Because the coefficients were chosen uniformly, the conditional distribution of the secret is unchanged after seeing any r−1 discs. This proves the Perfect secrecy of Shamir's threshold scheme.

i OurBigBook.com
A context-free grammar is a quadruple G=(V,Σ,P,S) consisting of a finite set V of nonterminal symbols, a disjoint finite alphabet Σ of terminal symbols, a start symbol S∈V, and a finite set P of productions A→α with A∈V and α∈(V∪Σ)∗. A sentence is a terminal word over an alphabet w∈Σ∗ with S⇒∗w, and the generated formal language is L(G)={w∈Σ∗:S⇒∗w}.
The first language is context-free. For example, the productions
S→aaSbb∣ε
(9)
generate exactly {a2mb2m:m≥0}: each recursive production adds two as to the left and two bs to the right.

ii

Words: 102 Articles: 1
4F OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 102
ii OurBigBook.com
The language L={am2bm2:m≥0} is not context-free. Suppose it had pumping length p in the pumping lemma for context-free languages, and apply the lemma to w=ap2bp2. Write w=uvxyz with ∣vxy∣≤p, ∣vy∣>0, and uvixyiz∈L for every i≥0.
Let α and β be the respective numbers of as and bs in vy. If α=β, pumping with i=0 or i=2 destroys equality of the two block lengths. Hence a valid decomposition would require α=β=d>0. Pumping with i=2 would then produce ap2+dbp2+d, where 1≤d≤p. But
p2<p2+d<(p+1)2,
(10)
so p2+d is not a square number. This contradiction proves the square-count language is not context-free.

At an endemic equilibrium, I∗>0, so 0=I˙=I∗(βS∗−γ) forces
S∗=βγ​.
(19)
The equation R˙=0 gives R∗=γI∗/α. The conservation law S∗+I∗+R∗=N therefore yields
I∗=β(α+γ)α(βN−γ)​,R∗=β(α+γ)γ(βN−γ)​.
(20)
A positive endemic state exists exactly when βN>γ, equivalently when the basic reproduction number R0​=βN/γ exceeds one.

Eliminate R=N−S−I to obtain the two-dimensional autonomous differential equation
S˙=α(N−S−I)−βSI,I˙=βSI−γI.
(21)
Its Jacobian matrix at the endemic equilibrium is
J∗​=(−α−βI∗βI∗​−α−γ0​).

trJ∗​=−(α+βI∗)<0,detJ∗​=βI∗(α+γ)>0.

The trace-determinant stability criterion shows that both eigenvalues have negative real part. The Endemic equilibrium of the SIR model with waning immunity is therefore locally asymptotically stable.

(z−ω)21​−ω21​=∑k=1∞​(k+1)ωk+2zk​.
(24)
Pairing ω with −ω cancels every odd power. Hence the Laurent series of the Weierstrass elliptic function is
℘(z)=z21​+3z2∑ω=0​ω−4+5z4∑ω=0​ω−6+O(z6)=z21​+20g2​​z2+28g3​​z4+O(z6),

Set
F(z)=℘′(z)2−4℘(z)3+g2​℘(z)+g3​.
(26)
This is an elliptic function. Write a=g2​/20 and b=g3​/28 in the expansion from part (i). At a lattice point, the coefficient of z−2 in F is g2​−20a=0, and its constant coefficient is g3​−28b=0; there are no other singular terms. Every apparent pole is therefore a removable singularity, and F extends to an entire elliptic function with value zero at the lattice points.
An entire elliptic function is bounded on a fundamental parallelogram and hence everywhere. By Liouville theorem it is constant, and its value at zero is zero. Thus F≡0, proving the Weierstrass elliptic differential equation
℘′(z)2=4℘(z)3−g2​℘(z)−g3​.​
(27)

Solution

Words: 142
8B OurBigBook.com
The repulsive force is F=kr/r3=−∇(k/r), so the Hamiltonian is
H=2mp2​+rk​.
(28)
The Hamilton's equations give r˙=p/m and p˙​=kr/r3. Consequently
L˙=r˙×p+r×p˙​=0,
(29)
so the angular momentum is conserved. Moreover,
p˙​×L=k(r3r(r⋅p)​−rp​)=−mkdtdr​.
(30)
It follows that the Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector A=p×L+mkr is conserved. By the Hamiltonian conservation law, these time derivatives are exactly {L,H} and {A,H}, so both Poisson brackets vanish.
The integrals of motion are the energy H, the components of L, and the components of A, subject to
A⋅L=0,A2=m2k2+2mHL2.
(31)
Taking the dot product of A with r gives
Acosθ=rL2​+mk.
(32)
Therefore the polar equation of a repulsive inverse-square orbit is
r=(A/(mk))cosθ−1L2/(mk)​=ecosθ−1λ​,
(33)
where λ=L2/(mk)≥0 and e=A/(mk)≥0. For a nonradial physical scattering orbit H>0, the identity above gives e>1, as expected for a hyperbolic Kepler orbit.

Choose U to prepare the uniform superposition, so the marked-state probability is p=1/4. Apply the marked-state phase oracle Rgπ​, followed by the reflection UR00π​U† about the prepared state. (px​)=⎩⎨⎧​0,1,−1,​p∣x,x≡0(modp) is a <quadratic residue>,x is a <quadratic nonresidue>.​

(px​)(px−1​)=(p1​)=1.

Gauss lemma states that if p∤a and m of the least positive residues of
a,2a,…,2p−1​a
(44)
exceed p/2, then (a/p)=(−1)m.
To prove it, replace each residue exceeding p/2 by its negative, obtaining numbers r1​,…,r(p−1)/2​ in {1,…,(p−1)/2}. No two of them are equal modulo p: such an equality would give ia≡±ja(modp), hence i=j in the allowed range. They therefore permute 1,…,(p−1)/2, and multiplication gives
a(p−1)/2(2p−1​)!≡(−1)m(2p−1​)!(modp).
(45)
Cancel the nonzero factorial and apply Euler's criterion to obtain the lemma.
For a=−1, all (p−1)/2 least positive residues p−1,p−2,…,(p+1)/2 exceed p/2. Hence the first supplementary law for quadratic reciprocity is
(p−1​)=(−1)(p−1)/2.​
(46)

Write χ(x)=(x/p). Choose a quadratic nonresidue a. Multiplication by a permutes Fp​, while multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol gives χ(ax)=−χ(x). Therefore
∑x∈Fp​​χ(x)=∑x∈Fp​​χ(ax)=−∑x∈Fp​​χ(x),
(47)
so the complete Legendre-symbol sum is zero.
Since 4x(x+1)=(2x+1)2−1 and χ(4)=1, the bijection x↦2x+1 reduces the next sum to ∑y​χ(y2−1). Count pairs (y,t)∈Fp2​ satisfying t2=y2−1. On one hand their number is
∑y​(1+χ(y2−1)).
(48)
On the other hand (y−t)(y+t)=1, and every u∈Fp×​ gives exactly one pair by y−t=u, y+t=u−1. There are therefore p−1 pairs, proving the quadratic Legendre-symbol correlation
∑x∈Fp​​χ(x(x+1))=−1.
(49)
For 1≤z≤p−2, the indicator that both z and z+1 are quadratic residues is (1+χ(z))(1+χ(z+1))/4. Summing and using the two identities above gives the number of consecutive nonzero quadratic residues modulo an odd prime
41​(p−2−χ(−1)−1−1)=4p−4−(−1)(p−1)/2​​.

A deterministic finite automaton is a tuple (Q,Σ,δ,q0​,F) with finite state set Q, finite input alphabet Σ, transition function δ:Q×Σ→Q, initial state q0​, and accepting-state set F⊆Q. It accepts a word when the extended transition function of a deterministic finite automaton carries q0​ to a state in F. A regular language is a language accepted by some deterministic finite automaton.
The pumping lemma for regular languages says that if a regular language is accepted by an automaton with N states, every accepted word w of length at least N has a decomposition w=xyz with ∣xy∣≤N, ∣y∣>0, and xyiz in the language for every i≥0. Indeed, among the N+1 states visited before and after the first N symbols, two are equal by the pigeonhole principle. The intervening nonempty word y labels a loop, which may be traversed any number of times without changing the final accepting state.
In base two, the powers of two have representations 10n, so their language is the regular expression 10∗ and is regular.
Suppose instead that their base-ten representations formed a regular language. Apply the pumping lemma to a sufficiently long decimal power of two xyz, and put d=∣y∣>0. Pumping gives decimal integers ai​ represented by xyiz, all powers of two. A direct place-value calculation shows that
ai+1​−10dai​=C
(51)
for a constant C independent of i. The lengths, and hence the exponents in ai​=2ni​, tend to infinity. Dividing by ai​ gives
2ni+1​−ni​−10d=2ni​C​.
(52)
For large i, the right side has absolute value less than one while the left side is an integer, so it must vanish. This would make a power of two equal to 10d=2d5d, impossible for d>0 by unique prime factorization. Thus the decimal powers of two are not a regular language.

Turan theorem states that among all N-vertex graphs containing no Kr+1​, the maximum number of edges is attained by the Turan graph Tr​(N), the complete multipartite graph whose r part sizes differ by at most one.
Here is the Zykov symmetrization proof. Start with an extremal Kr+1​-free graph. If nonadjacent vertices u,v have different neighbourhoods, replace the lower-degree vertex by a clone of the higher-degree one: delete all its incident edges and join it to precisely the neighbours of the other vertex. This does not decrease the number of edges and cannot create a Kr+1​, because a clique using the clone corresponds to one using the original vertex. Repeating the operation, with the standard tie-breaking that merges equal-neighbourhood classes, produces a complete multipartite extremal graph. It has at most r nonempty parts, since choosing one vertex from each part gives a clique.
If two part sizes satisfy a≥b+2, moving one vertex from the larger part to the smaller changes the number of cross-edges by
a−b−1>0.
(79)
Thus an extremal partition has exactly r parts whose sizes differ by at most one. This is Tr​(N) and proves the theorem. For r=2 it is Mantel theorem: a triangle-free graph on N vertices has at most ⌊N2/4⌋ edges.

A measure-preserving transformation T on a probability space (X,A,m) is ergodic if every invariant event A∈A, meaning
T−1A=A
(156)
up to an m-null set, satisfies m(A)∈{0,1}. Thus the invariant sigma-algebra is trivial modulo null sets.

The Kolmogorov zero-one law says that for independent random variables (Yn​)n≥0​, every event in the tail sigma-algebra
T=⋂N≥0​σ(YN​,YN+1​,…)

has probability zero or one.
In the canonical model of an independent and identically distributed sequence, the sample space is a sequence space EN with the product law, Yn​ is the nth coordinate, and the left Bernoulli shift S satisfies Yn​∘S=Yn+1​. If A is shift-invariant, then for every N,
A=S−NA∈σ(YN​,YN+1​,…),
(158)
so A∈T. The zero-one law therefore says that the canonical one-sided i.i.d. shift is ergodic.

The First Lyapunov theorem says that the existence of such a function makes the origin Lyapunov stable. To prove it, choose a sufficiently small closed ball Bε​⊂E. By compactness and positive definiteness,
α=min∥x∥=ε​V(x)>0.
(201)
By continuity, some δ>0 satisfies V(x)<α whenever ∥x∥<δ. Along a trajectory beginning in Bδ​, V cannot increase. Such a trajectory therefore cannot reach the sphere ∥x∥=ε, where V≥α. Hence it remains in Bε​ for every t≥0, which is Lyapunov stability.
The LaSalle invariance principle says that if a trajectory remains in a compact positively invariant set on which V˙≤0, then it approaches the largest invariant subset of {x:V˙(x)=0}.

To obtain a basin estimate from a Lyapunov sublevel set, take the largest sublevel component around the origin that remains inside the strict-decrease rectangle. On its boundary ∣x∣=2​ or ∣y∣=π/2, the minimum value of V is 1. Hence the maximal open estimate is
DV​={(x,y):∣y∣<2π​, 2x2​+sin2y<1}​.
(211)
Every smaller closed sublevel set V≤c<1 is compact and positively invariant, and V˙<0 there except at the origin. The LaSalle invariance principle therefore implies convergence to the origin. Taking the union over c<1 shows that DV​ lies in the domain of stability. No larger sublevel component can be certified from this V alone, because every level c>1 contains points (0,y) just beyond ∣y∣=π/2 where V˙>0.

A boson is an identical particle whose total multiparticle quantum state is symmetric under exchange of any two particles, whereas a fermion has a total state that is antisymmetric under every exchange. The Spin-statistics theorem associates integer spin with bosons and half-integer spin with fermions.
For three distinguishable spin-one particles, the spin Hilbert space has dimension
33=27.
(232)
Let
S=S1​+S2​+S3​
(233)
be the total angular momentum operator. Since each particle has
Si2​=1(1+1)ℏ2=2ℏ2,
(234)
we have
S2=6ℏ2+2(S1​⋅S2​+S2​⋅S3​+S3​⋅S1​).
(235)
The Hamiltonian operator is consequently
H=ℏ2λ​(S2−6ℏ2).
(236)
On the total-spin sector with quantum number J, its energy eigenvalue is
EJ​=λ[J(J+1)−6].
(237)
The Clebsch-Gordan decomposition may be performed by first coupling particles 1 and 2. Their intermediate spin is j12​=0,1,2, and coupling the third spin gives
j12​012​J10,1,21,2,3.​​
(238)
Thus the three spin-one angular-momentum decomposition contains total spin J=0,1,2,3 with multiplicities 1,3,2,1. Multiplying each multiplicity by the multiplet dimension 2J+1 gives
J0123​EJ​−6λ−4λ06λ​degeneracy19107.​​
(239)
The degeneracies sum to 27, as required.
When the particles are indistinguishable, their integer spin makes them bosons. Their common spatial wavefunction is symmetric, so their spin wavefunction must also lie in the symmetric three-spin-one subspace. Its decomposition is
Sym3(1)=3⊕1.
(240)
Hence only the J=3 and J=1 levels remain, now with one copy of each multiplet:
E=−4λ has degeneracy 3,E=6λ has degeneracy 7.​
(241)

For c=+arcosh5, F decreases directly from 0 to −1, matching flow everywhere toward the sink. For the negative root, F initially becomes positive and creates a reverse-flow region next to the wall. The physically likely choice is therefore
c=+arcosh5​.
(318)

Use the Fourier transform convention
η​(k,t)=∫−∞∞​η(x,t)e−ikxdx,η(x,t)=2π1​∫−∞∞​η​(k,t)eikxdk.
(319)
The deep-water capillary-wave dispersion relation makes each Fourier mode satisfy
∂t2​η​+S2∣k∣3η​=0.
(320)
The transformed initial data are
η​(k,0)=0,∂t​η​(k,0)=−W∫−ϵϵ​e−ikxdx=−k2Wsin(kϵ)​.
(321)
Therefore
η​(k,t)=−kS∣k∣3/22Wsin(kϵ)​sin(S∣k∣3/2t).
(322)
The integrand is even, so Fourier inversion gives the surface response to a localized impulsive velocity
η(x,t)=−πS2W​∫0∞​k5/2sin(kϵ)sin(Sk3/2t)cos(kx)​dk​.
(323)

Put x=Vt with fixed V>0. The relevant stationary point will have k=O(V2/S2), so the assumption ϵV2/S2≪1 allows the long-wave approximation
sin(kϵ)∼kϵ.
(324)
Using sinAcosB=[sin(A+B)+sin(A−B)]/2, the phase Sk3/2+Vk has no stationary point for k>0. The other phase is
ϕ(k)=Sk3/2−Vk,
(325)
with
ϕ′(k0​)=0,k0​=9S24V2​,
(326)
and
ϕ(k0​)=−27S24V3​,ϕ′′(k0​)=8V9S2​>0.
(327)
The stationary part of the integral is therefore
−πSWϵ​∫0∞​k−3/2sin[tϕ(k)]dk.
(328)
By the one-dimensional stationary-phase formula, this is asymptotic to
−πSWϵ​k0−3/2​tϕ′′(k0​)2π​​sin(tϕ(k0​)+4π​).
(329)
Since
k0−3/2​tϕ′′(k0​)2π​​=2V5/2t​9S2π​​,
(330)
we obtain
η(x,t)∼2π​V5/2t​9WϵS​sin(27S24V3t​−4π​).
(331)
Using V=x/t, this has the requested form
η(x,t)∼x5/2WϵSt2​F(S2t2x3​)​,
(332)
where
F(q)=2π​9​sin(274q​−4π​)​.
(333)

The stationary contribution travels with group velocity
V=ω′(k0​)=23S​k0​​,
(334)
so k0​=4V2/(9S2). The condition
S2ϵV2​≪1
(335)
is therefore equivalent, up to a constant factor, to k0​ϵ≪1: the dominant wavelength is much longer than the impacted interval. Its Fourier transform can then be replaced by
−k2Wsin(kϵ)​∼−2Wϵ,
(336)
which is the total initial vertical velocity integrated over space. The far field cannot resolve W and ϵ separately and depends only on their product Wϵ.

a OurBigBook.com
A complex square matrix A is a normal matrix if it commutes with its conjugate transpose:
AA∗=A∗A.
(337)
By unitary diagonalization of a normal matrix, there are a unitary matrix U and a diagonal matrix Λ=diag(λ1​,…,λN​) such that
A=UΛU∗.
(338)
The matrix 2-norm is invariant under multiplication by unitary matrices, so
∥A∥2​=∥Λ∥2​.
(339)
For a diagonal matrix,
∥Λx∥22​=∑j​∣λj​∣2∣xj​∣2≤(maxj​∣λj​∣2)∥x∥22​,
(340)
with equality on a coordinate vector belonging to an eigenvalue of greatest modulus. Hence
∥A∥2​=jmax​∣λj​∣=ρ(A)​,
(341)
the matrix 2-norm of a normal matrix.

b

Words: 111 Articles: 1
40E OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 111
b OurBigBook.com
Let D∈RM×M be the Toeplitz antisymmetric tridiagonal matrix with Dm,m+1​=1, Dm,m−1​=−1, and zero diagonal. Fixed homogeneous endpoint values give the homogeneous update
(I−4μ​D)un+1=(I+4μ​D)un.
(342)
The hint gives the eigenvalues
dj​=2icosM+1jπ​,1≤j≤M.
(343)
Because each dj​ is purely imaginary, 1−(μ/4)dj​=0 for every real μ, so the left matrix is invertible. The two matrices are polynomials in D and therefore have the same orthonormal eigenvectors. The amplification matrix
Q=(I−4μ​D)−1(I+4μ​D)
(344)
has eigenvalues
qj​=1−i(μ/2)cos(jπ/(M+1))1+i(μ/2)cos(jπ/(M+1))​.
(345)
The numerator and denominator are complex conjugates, so ∣qj​∣=1. Moreover, the common orthonormal eigenbasis makes Q a normal matrix. By the matrix 2-norm of a normal matrix,
∥Qn∥2​=ρ(Qn)=1
(346)
for every n. Thus the Crank-Nicolson centered-advection scheme on a finite interval is unconditionally stable:
every μ>0.​
(347)

c

Words: 153 Articles: 1
40E OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 153
c OurBigBook.com
Insert the Fourier mode
umn​=ζneimθ
(348)
into the leapfrog advection scheme. This gives
ζn+1=μ(eiθ−e−iθ)ζn+ζn−1,
(349)
and hence the amplification polynomial
ζ2−2iμsinθζ−1=0.
(350)
Its roots are
ζ±​=iμsinθ±1−μ2sin2θ​.
(351)
If 0<μ<1, the square root is real for every θ, and
∣ζ±​∣2=μ2sin2θ+1−μ2sin2θ=1.
(352)
If μ>1, choosing ∣sinθ∣>1/μ makes the roots non-real multiples of i with reciprocal moduli, one of which exceeds one, so the method is unstable.
The endpoint μ=1 requires care. At θ=π/2 the polynomial is
(ζ−i)2,
(353)
so a generic mode has the form (c1​+c2​n)in and grows linearly. It satisfies the weaker test ∣ζ±​∣≤1 often quoted in elementary Fourier analysis, but it violates the root condition for a multistep method because the unit-modulus root is repeated. Therefore the rigorous uniform stability range for arbitrary two-level initial data is
0<μ<1​.
(354)
If “stable” is being used only for the non-amplification condition on root moduli, the conventionally quoted range is 0<μ≤1, with μ=1 a defective marginal endpoint rather than a uniformly stable case.
